results.question: Compare the binary-population plans in "Globular Clusters in the Time of the JWST. I. Survey Design and First Results on Multiple Populations and Beyond" with the reported classifier results in "Unresolved Binary Systems in the Rubin Era I: An Autoencoder Framework for Binary Identification Applied to 47 Tucanae". (a) Which binary-population properties does the JWST survey plan to refine, including its treatment of 1P and 2P? (b) What binary-class precision and completeness does the autoencoder study report on its test set at threshold 0.5, and what does the bimodal prediction distribution suggest? Explain why these classifier metrics are not themselves a measured cluster binary fraction. Cite both papers.
results.reference_answer: The JWST survey plans to refine binary fractions, mass-ratio distributions and radial segregation using its CMDs, and to estimate binary fractions separately for different populations, including 1P and 2P. It motivates this separation by the hypothesis that 2P formed in denser environments with more efficient binary disruption. The autoencoder study reports binary-class test-set precision 0.87 and completeness 0.81 at threshold 0.5; its often bimodal predictions indicate confidence in classifying targets as single or binary. Precision/completeness describe classifier performance on the test set, not the proportion of cluster stars that are binaries. They do not replace the survey's population-fraction measurements or establish the 1P-versus-2P hypothesis.

However, while the aforementioned ML models are very powerful, they are also typically tailored to identify specific binary populations or use specialized datasets. Furthermore, many of these techniques are also restrictive, which means that genuinely novel or unexpected events may go undetected. This highlights a gap in the field. There is a need for a classification technique that has all the advantages of CMD-based methods (i.e., fast and cheap) that uses all available filters and colors, yet remains versatile enough to adapt to any type of stellar population. In this work, we present `flexAE` , a novel and flexible ML approach to identifying binary stars that is based on a autoencoder (AE) framework that satisfies all criteria mentioned above. 

The need for such a framework has become particularly apparent with the recent commencement of the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSST. ## ABSTRACT 

Binary systems are extremely common and influence many areas of astrophysics, such as stellar evolution and cluster dynamics. In this work, we introduce `flexAE` , a framework that combines a classical autoencoder architecture with a dedicated classifier component. It is designed to distinguish between single stars and binary systems based on their broadband spectral energy distributions, using all available photometry simultaneously while accounting for observational uncertainties. We demonstrate the capability of `flexAE` by using it to identify unresolved main sequence binaries in the outskirts of the 47 Tucanae globular cluster (NGC 104) with photometric data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. We train the model on a simulated sample of single star and binary systems created with stellar atmosphere models. The model accurately reconstructs the photometric input features and achieves a classification accuracy of 0.85 on the simulated test set. We then apply the trained model to a sample of 1,424 cluster members found in Rubin DP1 with reliable _gri_ photometry, of which 32 are identified by the model as unresolved main sequence binaries. This corresponds to an observed binary fraction of 2 _._ 2[+0] _−_ 0 _[.] ._[5] 3[%.][We][estimate][that][the][intrinsic][main][sequence][binary][fraction][lies][between][3] _[.]_[7][+0] _−_ 0 _[.] ._[8] 5[%][and] 7 _._ 5[+1] _−_ 1 _[.] ._[5] 1[%.][The][binary][fraction][stays][constant][between][18] _[ −]_[36][arcmin][(5] _[.]_[7] _[ −]_[11] _[.]_[4][half-light][radii)][from] the cluster center. We highlight that `flexAE` can be easily adapted for other use cases. This makes `flexAE` well-suited for large-scale binary classification in upcoming wide-field surveys, such as Rubin LSST. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/tobiasgeron/flexAE.

These properties are essential for understanding GC dynamical evolution and the formation of exotic stellar populations, such as blue straggler stars, cataclysmic variables, millisecond pulsars, and low-mass X-ray binaries. 

We will exploit the CMDs presented in this work to refine measurements of the binary fraction, mass-ratio distribution, and radial segregation, extending previous studies (Milone et al. 2012a), which were largely limited to cluster inner regions. We will also estimate the binary fraction for different stellar populations following the methodology introduced in our previous works (Milone et al. 2020, 2025b; Bortolan et al. 2025). Measuring the binary fraction separately for 1P and 2P stars is particularly important, as 2P stars likely formed in denser environments where binaries are more efficiently disrupted. results.answer:
The JWST survey paper states it will refine measurements of the binary fraction, the mass-ratio distribution, and the radial (radial segregation) distribution of binaries in globular clusters. [1]

The JWST survey paper says it will estimate the binary fraction separately for different stellar populations and specifically measure the binary fraction for 1P and 2P stars, because 2P stars likely formed in denser environments where binaries are more efficiently disrupted. [1]

The autoencoder study reports that, on its test set using a threshold y > 0.5, the precision for the binary class is 0.87 and the completeness is 0.81. [2]

The autoencoder study reports that the distribution of predicted outputs is 'very bimodal', which 'suggests that the model is often confident that the target is either a single star (low yhat) or a binary system (high yhat)'. [2]

The autoencoder study reports that using a stricter threshold y > 0.9 changes the binary-class precision and completeness on the test set to 0.98 and 0.60, respectively. [2]

When applied to 47 Tucanae Rubin DP1 members with a conservative threshold y > 0.9, the autoencoder study finds an observed MS+MS binary fraction of 2.2% in the outskirts and explicitly describes this value as a lower limit because lower mass-ratio binary systems were likely missed. [3]

The autoencoder study's sample-selection procedure included filtering Rubin DP1 objects within 2 degrees, removing extended sources, PSF failures, blended objects, excluding objects within 18 arcmin of the cluster center, and cross-matching with Gaia DR3 to ensure cluster membership. [4]

Precision and completeness reported on the model's test set are classification-performance metrics on labeled data and are not by themselves a measured cluster binary fraction, which requires applying the classifier to a selected sample of cluster members and accounting for missed systems and selection effects (as the autoencoder paper both applied selection/membership filtering and treated the observed fraction as a lower limit). claims.text: The JWST survey paper states it will refine measurements of the binary fraction, the mass-ratio distribution, and the radial (radial segregation) distribution of binaries in globular clusters.

The JWST survey paper says it will estimate the binary fraction separately for different stellar populations and specifically measure the binary fraction for 1P and 2P stars, because 2P stars likely formed in denser environments where binaries are more efficiently disrupted.
The autoencoder study reports that, on its test set using a threshold y > 0.5, the precision for the binary class is 0.87 and the completeness is 0.81.

The autoencoder study reports that the distribution of predicted outputs is 'very bimodal', which 'suggests that the model is often confident that the target is either a single star (low yhat) or a binary system (high yhat)'.
The autoencoder study reports that using a stricter threshold y > 0.9 changes the binary-class precision and completeness on the test set to 0.98 and 0.60, respectively.

When applied to 47 Tucanae Rubin DP1 members with a conservative threshold y > 0.9, the autoencoder study finds an observed MS+MS binary fraction of 2.2% in the outskirts and explicitly describes this value as a lower limit because lower mass-ratio binary systems were likely missed.

The autoencoder study's sample-selection procedure included filtering Rubin DP1 objects within 2 degrees, removing extended sources, PSF failures, blended objects, excluding objects within 18 arcmin of the cluster center, and cross-matching with Gaia DR3 to ensure cluster membership.

Precision and completeness reported on the model's test set are classification-performance metrics on labeled data and are not by themselves a measured cluster binary fraction, which requires applying the classifier to a selected sample of cluster members and accounting for missed systems and selection effects (as the autoencoder paper both applied selection/membership filtering and treated the observed fraction as a lower limit).
